reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's OMMBID
clinicalPearls: Dominated by progressive neurodegeneration and severe behavioural disturbance, with comparatively mild somatic and skeletal features
Comprises four biochemical subtypes (A, B, C, D), each from deficiency of a distinct enzyme in the heparan sulfate degradation pathway
Typical course is an initial period of near-normal development followed by developmental regression, hyperactivity, aggression, and sleep disturbance
Coarse facial features and organomegaly are subtle compared with other mucopolysaccharidoses, which frequently delays diagnosis
Only heparan sulfate accumulates and is excreted in excess, unlike the mixed glycosaminoglycan pattern of MPS I and II
Enzyme assays identify the specific subtype after urinary heparan sulfate points to the diagnosis
Progressive dementia, seizures, and loss of mobility mark the later stages
reference.pathophysiology: Sanfilippo syndrome is caused by deficiency of one of four lysosomal enzymes required for the sequential degradation of heparan sulfate: heparan-N-sulfatase (type A, SGSH), alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase (type B, NAGLU), acetyl-CoA:alpha-glucosaminide N-acetyltransferase (type C, HGSNAT), and N-acetylglucosamine-6-sulfatase (type D, GNS). The resulting block leads to lysosomal accumulation of heparan sulfate, which is particularly toxic to neurons, producing the profound central nervous system degeneration that characterises the disorder. Somatic tissues are relatively spared because dermatan sulfate metabolism is intact. Excess heparan sulfate is excreted in the urine. All four subtypes are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and are clinically indistinguishable, requiring enzymatic or molecular testing to separate them.
additionalDifferentials: Other mucopolysaccharidoses, especially Hunter syndrome (MPS II)
Idiopathic autism spectrum disorder or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Rett syndrome and other neurodevelopmental regression disorders
Other lysosomal storage disorders with dementia
Non-syndromic intellectual disability with behavioural problems
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urinary glycosaminoglycan analysis showing isolated heparan sulfate elevation
Enzyme assays for the four candidate enzymes to determine subtype
Molecular testing of SGSH, NAGLU, HGSNAT, or GNS genes
Brain MRI to document white matter and atrophic changes
Developmental and neuropsychological assessment to track regression
redFlags: Progressive developmental regression after a period of normal milestones
Escalating behavioural disturbance with severe sleep disruption
Loss of ambulation and swallowing difficulty in later stages
reference.prognosis: The disorder is relentlessly progressive, with most patients declining into severe dementia and immobility, and survival typically limited to the second or third decade. No disease-modifying therapy is established, so management is supportive.
pitfalls: Attributing early behavioural symptoms solely to a primary neurodevelopmental disorder and missing the storage disease
Expecting prominent coarse facies or organomegaly and dismissing the diagnosis when they are mild
Relying on a single enzyme assay without confirming the specific subtype
Overlooking heparan sulfate on urinary screening if only total glycosaminoglycan is measured
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
